---
title: "Choosing a mixture with BIC"
---

A Gaussian mixture requires a component count and covariance structure. Adding components or covariance parameters usually improves maximized likelihood on the observations used to fit them. The largest fitted likelihood thus rewards flexibility even when the added structure does not recur.

The earlier page on [information criteria](../model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.qmd#compare-aic-with-bic) introduced the [**Bayesian information criterion (BIC)**](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html) as maximized likelihood plus a parameter-count penalty. This page applies that criterion to mixture specifications. We declare the candidates, calculate the penalty, and interpret what the resulting comparison can and cannot establish about linguistic categories.

## State the candidate specifications

A mixture candidate includes more than the number of components $K$. It also includes the covariance restriction, feature representation, preprocessing rule, initialization policy, and fitting controls.

Write one candidate as

$$
M
=
\langle K,\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}\rangle,
$$

where $\mathcal{C}$ is the covariance family and $\mathcal{R}$ records the remaining fitting procedure. Comparing $K=2$ and $K=3$ while silently changing scaling would not isolate component count.

The candidate set should be declared before the final comparison. Searching many unreported specifications and presenting one favorable result makes the analytical search disappear from the report.

## See why fitted likelihood favors flexibility

A larger mixture can often reproduce a smaller mixture by assigning negligible weight to an added component or by duplicating existing parameters. It may then improve fit by adapting the new component to a subset of observations.

Thus, maximized likelihood tends to increase as the candidate becomes more flexible. The same observations select the component parameters and reward the selected fit.

The improvement may represent a recurring distributional pattern. It may also represent a small irregular group or a nearly collapsed covariance. Fit diagnostics must rule out invalid solutions before any information criterion is interpreted.

## Calculate BIC

For maximized likelihood $L$, $q$ estimated parameters, and $n$ observations, define

$$
\operatorname{BIC}
=
-2\log L+q\log n.
$$

Lower values are preferred under this definition. The first term rewards fitted likelihood. The second penalizes parameter count.

Suppose a three-component model reduces $-2\log L$ by 18 relative to a two-component model but introduces six parameters. With $n=100$, the added penalty is

$$
6\log(100)
\approx
6(4.605)
=
27.63.
$$

The change from the smaller model to the larger model is

$$
\Delta\operatorname{BIC}
=
-18+27.63
=
9.63.
$$

The larger model has a BIC about 9.63 units higher, so the smaller model is preferred under the stated definition. The likelihood improvement is not large enough to offset the additional penalty.

## Implement the criterion directly

```{r}
#| eval: false

candidate <- data.frame(
  model = c("two components", "three components"),
  minus_two_log_likelihood = c(400, 382),
  parameters = c(8, 14)
)

n_observations <- 100

candidate$bic <-
  candidate$minus_two_log_likelihood +
  candidate$parameters * log(n_observations)

candidate
```

Some software reports the negative of this expression and treats larger values as better. Check the package definition before comparing signs. Within one analysis, do not combine values produced under opposite conventions.

## Interpret the sample size

BIC uses $n$ inside the penalty. Repeated linguistic data make the meaning of that quantity important.

The Peterson and Barney table contains 1,520 vowel tokens from 76 speakers. Setting $n=1520$ counts observed token rows in the likelihood. It does not imply that 1,520 unrelated speakers were sampled. Each speaker contributes repeated vowel tokens.

Thus, a BIC comparison can rank fitted mixture specifications for the declared token likelihood without licensing a population claim that treats each token as an independent speaker. The criterion answers a relative model-selection question under the fitted likelihood. It does not repair a sampling design.

## Interpret the candidate set

BIC compares only the candidates supplied to it. A two-component model preferred over a three-component model has not been preferred over every possible representation, covariance family, or component count.

Mixtures also complicate the regularity assumptions behind simple information-criterion arguments. Component labels can be permuted without changing the observation density, and parameters can become weakly identified when a component has little mass.

These concerns do not make the printed comparison meaningless. They limit the claim. Report the complete candidate definitions, convergence checks, and any near-degenerate solutions before interpreting the selected value.

## Keep components separate from categories

Suppose the smallest BIC occurs at ten components for the ten intended Peterson and Barney vowel words. That numerical match does not show that BIC discovered the phonological inventory.

One vowel may require more than one Gaussian region because speakers differ. Several intended vowels may overlap within one component under the selected acoustic representation. Intended vowel labels should thus be used after fitting to describe alignment and uncertain tokens. They should not determine the mixture likelihood being compared.

## Check the BIC comparison

1. Why does maximized likelihood tend to favor more flexible mixtures?
2. How is the BIC change 9.63 obtained in the worked comparison?
3. Which BIC sign convention is used on this page?
4. What belongs in a declared mixture specification besides $K$?
5. Why does $n=1520$ not mean that 1,520 unrelated speakers were sampled?
6. Why need the selected component count not equal the number of intended vowels?
7. What fit problems should be checked before interpreting BIC?

## What BIC establishes

BIC ranks declared mixture specifications by combining maximized likelihood with a parameter-count penalty. The ranking remains conditional on the candidate set, response representation, likelihood, sample-size convention, and fitting validity. A preferred mixture is a supported distributional summary, not a discovered inventory of phonological categories.

The [next page](validating-a-mixture.qmd) asks a different question by scoring predictions for observations excluded from fitting.
